title: A Pro-Russia Strongman at Mar-a-Lago
summary: In the days after Tuesday’s midterm elections, luminaries of the MAGA movement will gather at Mar-a-Lago to turn their attention to 2028. Speakers will include a Cabinet secretary, the head of the Domestic Policy Council, and several members of Congress. Also present will be Milorad Dodik, the pro-R...
content:
In the days after Tuesday’s midterm elections, luminaries of the MAGA movement will gather at Mar-a-Lago to turn their attention to 2028. Speakers will include a Cabinet secretary, the head of the Domestic Policy Council, and several members of Congress. Also present will be Milorad Dodik, the pro-Russia strongman who has bragged about spying on Americans and recently called Russian President Vladimir Putin “one of the most peace-loving leaders of our time.” Dodik is the de facto leader of Bosnia’s Serb population, concentrated in a political entity called Republika Srpska within Bosnia and Herzegovina. His push for secession risks reigniting bloody sectarian conflict in the Balkans.

Dodik’s travel plans were described to me by several people familiar with them. These people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preview nonpublic matters, said the details could change at the last minute. (His office did not respond to a request for comment.) But Dodik’s expected attendance reflects his reversal of fortune under the Trump administration, the success of a pricey foreign lobbying campaign, and a further alignment of American and Russian interests.

Republika Srpska paid two of Trump’s top political advisers, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, as consultants and brought them to the Serb-majority political entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina for elections earlier this month. (They later donated their earnings to Trump’s presidential library fund after news of the work became public and the president lashed out at them on Truth Social.) When his party won a decisive result, Dodik credited both Trump and Putin for their support. “If it had not been for Donald Trump’s magnificent victory,” Dodik told supporters after the favorable result, “we would probably be political corpses today.”

In 2022, the Biden administration sanctioned Dodik for what the Treasury Department called “graft,” “corruption,” and “bribery,” as well as threats to the stability of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Balkan nation where ethnic divisions catalyzed a brutal war from 1992 to 1995. The conflict climaxed in the genocide at Srebrenica, which until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine was the most horrific mass murder in Europe since World War II. Dodik, according to the U.S. government, had attempted to sabotage the accords that ended the war, the Dayton peace agreement. He was accused of creating parallel state institutions in the federated country’s Serb-majority entity and of denigrating other ethnic and religious groups, above all Muslim Bosniaks. Numerous family members, allies, and companies were eventually also sanctioned. Formerly Srpska’s president, Dodik was stripped of that position and banned from holding office for six years after being convicted by the Bosnian judicial system last year of flouting decisions by the international envoy overseeing the Dayton Accords. He has rejected those decisions as politically motivated and void of constitutional authority, and continues to exercise near-total control over Srpska’s institutions.

Since Trump returned to office last year, the Srpska government has unleashed millions of dollars on lobbyists in a bid to burnish Dodik’s image with the people around Trump. The strategy has been to portray him as a martyr in the American president’s image—a victim of legal maneuvering and a crusader for Christian values holding back what some Serbian nationalists characterize as a tide of Muslim influence. Among those whose services Dodik and his allies have tapped are Rudy Giuliani, the president’s former personal lawyer; Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor who landed a pardon from Trump last year; and the firm employing Katie Wiles, the daughter of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

[Read: The Trump family sparks a revolution in Albania]

In October 2025, the Trump administration dropped the sanctions. The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control did not offer a rationale, but the State Department had days earlier hailed several conciliatory steps taken by Srpska’s legislative body as the result of Washington’s efforts to “defuse the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina.” State Department officials also pushed for the resignation of the international envoy who had clashed with Dodik. Christian Schmidt, a conservative German politician who had taken up the role of high representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2021, complied in May of this year, telling a German newspaper that he had come under “enormous and unexpected pressure from the U.S.”

Diplomats in the region as well as experts have viewed the Trump administration’s concessions to Dodik with significant alarm because of his avowed separatist aims and his explicit backing by Putin. Both Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are candidates for European Union membership.

The event planned for next week at Mar-a-Lago is an offshoot of the Conservative Political Action Conference, a right-wing jamboree that has enlarged its international footprint in recent years. It’s called the CPAC Circle Retreat and Gala and is billed as a “Gathering of Visionaries.” The website makes explicit the event’s connection with the next presidential election, stating, “As midterm election results come in, we’ll discuss what they mean for the political landscape and the road to 2028.” Speakers include the secretary of labor and at least two U.S. senators, Mike Lee of Utah and Rick Scott of Florida. Eduardo Bolsonaro, the brother of Flávio Bolsonaro, the failed Brazilian presidential candidate who recently arrived in the U.S. to evade possible prosecution on allegations of money laundering and tax evasion, is another advertised speaker. When I asked Matt Schlapp, the chairman of the American Conservative Union and CPAC’s host, about Dodik’s attendance, he told me, “We will have a very interesting group of donors and VIPs, but we won’t comment on who will be in attendance other than who the speakers will be.” He added that the “focus will be on America’s future heading into 2028.”

It’s not clear whether Trump will be at Mar-a-Lago during Dodik’s anticipated visit, but his presence there will take him into one of MAGA’s main nerve centers. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. During a visit to Washington earlier this year, Dodik had photo ops with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Karoline Leavitt, the then–White House press secretary.

Current and former U.S. officials told me that Dodik may feel pressure to achieve his aim of securing Srpska’s independence soon, given that Trump is likely to be friendlier to him than a potential Democratic successor after 2028. Tuesday’s election in the U.S. will help determine MAGA’s long-term political viability. No matter the result, Trump will have another two years to keep giving Dodik what he wants.

title: The Election Lies Are Already Starting on X
summary: Last weekend, Chaya Raichik, the popular right-wing influencer who goes by Libs of TikTok, made an ominous claim to her nearly 5 million followers on X. “In Minnesota, the USPS offices are inside mosques,” she wrote. “The people who handle mail-in ballots.. What are we doing America.” She reshared a...
content:
Last weekend, Chaya Raichik, the popular right-wing influencer who goes by Libs of TikTok, made an ominous claim to her nearly 5 million followers on X. “In Minnesota, the USPS offices are inside mosques,” she wrote. “The people who handle mail-in ballots.. What are we doing America.” She reshared a 28-minute-long video of a man circling a brick building in Plymouth, Minnesota, and accosting postal workers inside. “It’s the Islamification of the United States,” the man says. “And we have to stop it.”

Almost everything about Raichik’s post is misleading. The post office is not “inside” a mosque; they are housed in different sections of the same building. And there’s no reason to believe that the shared real estate has anything to do with the integrity of elections. In situations like this, X’s crowdsourced fact-checking feature, called “Community Notes,” is supposed to help correct the record. Users propose disclaimers for popular posts they believe are inaccurate, and if other users agree, the disclaimer gets attached to the post. Sure enough, the day after Raichik’s post, someone suggested slapping the post with a Community Note to clarify the facts, citing and linking to articles by The Minnesota Star Tribune and Minnesota Public Radio. But the note was never publicly shown on X. As of yesterday, the video had more than 1.7 million views. (Raichik did not respond to a request for comment.)

Since Elon Musk bought X four years ago, the platform has been a petri dish for rumors and propaganda. Now, having weathered a liberal exodus to other platforms, X could play a central role in the midterm elections—especially if Republicans fare poorly. X has become the go-to place for MAGA supporters to hunt for examples of voter fraud, which could be used to cast doubt on results that don’t go Republicans’ way. President Trump has endorsed this crusade—he recently announced a $1 million bounty for voter-fraud tips that lead to a conviction.

Community Notes, which even some of Musk’s critics have praised as a worthwhile program, would seem to offer a bulwark against bogus claims of vote-rigging. It’s built around a clever idea: Each proposed note gets rated “helpful” or “not helpful” by users who have disagreed about related past notes. X publishes only the notes on which the users have reached a consensus. Yet even though X has expanded the feature, bringing in AI note writers to work alongside the human volunteers, it’s proving stubbornly incapable of addressing most election-related falsehoods. If Tuesday and the days afterward bring widespread claims of rigged results, expect many of them to originate on X.

Since Musk embraced Community Notes on X, crowdsourced fact-checks have gone from a niche experiment to the default on social media. After Trump’s reelection, Meta ditched its partnerships with professional fact-checking organizations in the U.S. in favor of its own version of Community Notes. (Meta still uses professional fact-checks in other countries.) YouTube and TikTok have adopted similar features. But X’s version is the most established, and it has served as the industry’s model. In some respects, it works quite well: The system routinely corrects misleading posts about topics such as sports, pop culture, and advertising.

[Read: We’re back to the actually internet]

The problem is that it’s rare for liberals and conservatives to agree on notes that touch on the most polarizing topics—meaning that fact-checks about politics and elections rarely get approved. That has had predictable effects on the motivation of the program’s volunteers, Mike Doris, a longtime contributor to Community Notes, told me. A group chat where active members share information and sources has become a “ghost town,” Doris said. Some have given up; he is close to doing the same.

While humans might get discouraged, bots do not. To scale up the program, X has opened fact-checking to AI, creating a purpose-built agent powered by Grok and inviting outside researchers to build AI fact-checking tools of their own. It might seem ironic that the same technology that can generate falsehoods at scale is now being used to catch them. Yet the bots are more prolific, and X says that notes proposed by AI are also more likely to win approval from the masses, perhaps because they’re trained to use neutral language and cite reputable sources. What started as an experiment last year has quickly become the norm: In May, an analysis by The Indicator’s Alexios Mantzarlis found that half of all Community Notes shown on X are now written by just eight bot accounts. This month, the Georgetown University social-media researcher Renée DiResta analyzed X’s public research and found that six of those eight are controlled by the platform itself.

This has led to a Cambrian explosion in the total number of Community Notes on X. But when it comes to politics, bots haven’t fixed the fundamental problem: Users on the left and the right just can’t find common ground. The proposed note for Raichik’s post about the post office attached to the mosque was, in fact, written by an AI agent, though not one of X’s. NewsGuard, a company that tracks misinformation, found that 93 percent of false claims about the midterms on X failed to receive a Community Note. (DiResta’s own AI fact-checking bot, she told me, has proposed 81 Community Notes; only one has been approved.)

In the weeks before the election, many of these unchecked posts have involved false claims about candidates. Fake videos targeting at least three Democratic Senate candidates have been linked to Russian disinformation campaigns. One starts with a shot of a real Cleveland local-news reporter, then cuts to fabricated footage describing nonexistent claims of sexual misconduct against the Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown by women who used to work for him. Darren Linvill, a Clemson University professor who researches foreign-interference campaigns, told me that X has taken down some of the accounts behind the posts, but the same group of influencers on the platform keeps amplifying new ones. Of the 37 viral false claims about the midterms identified by NewsGuard’s ongoing tracker, 22 started as X posts, and many of them spread to larger platforms from there. Not all of them target Democratic candidates: One debunked post claims that the Texas Republican Ken Paxton paid for a billboard that read, Pedos ain’t that bad.

Fact-checks were never a cure-all for social-media lies. Many conservatives distrusted mainstream fact-checking organizations, and some research has shown that Community Notes are more broadly believed. A spokesperson for X told me that the addition of AI note writers has roughly doubled the number of Community Notes published in the past year. X, Meta, and other social-media companies also have rules against certain types of election misinformation, which they enforce through other means. For instance, X said earlier this month that it suspended more than 13,000 accounts linked to foreign-influence campaigns, and at least one viral post showing the satirical Paxton billboard now carries a “manipulated media” label.

Still, the limits of crowdsourced fact-checking might become obvious in the days to come. AI bots in particular are likely to struggle to counter fast-flying fraud claims on Election Day, DiResta pointed out. “The AI does not know what is happening on the ground unless a human has written it somewhere retrievable,” she said. In 2020, the last national election when Trump was in the White House, the president’s claims that the election had been stolen gained traction on social media and helped fuel the Capitol insurrection on January 6, 2021. Back then, Twitter applied numerous fact-checks and warning labels to posts by Trump and his allies making unsupported claims that the vote had been rigged. It’s hard to envision the platform doing that this time around.

content:
Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings, watch full episodes here, or listen to the weekly podcast here.

Tuesday’s midterm results could help determine what President Trump’s remaining two years in office will look like. On Washington Week With The Atlantic, panelists joined to discuss this and more.

The upcoming elections may be “coming down to Republicans,” Susan Glasser, a staff writer at The New Yorker, argued last night. It’s the “Republicans who believed Donald Trump when he said he was the president of no new wars, who believed Donald Trump when he said prices were going to come down on day one of his administration.”

Joining guest moderator Vivian Salama, a staff writer at The Atlantic, to discuss further: Peter Baker, a chief White House correspondent at The New York Times; Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report; Glasser; and Asma Khalid, the co-host of The Global Story podcast on BBC News.

Watch the full episode here.

title: The ‘Cuteservative’ in Chief
summary: Inside a podcast studio at Turning Point USA’s headquarters last month, a former witch sat in a pink velvet armchair, telling Alex Clark about the demon that stalked her house. Even though this self-described witch, known on TikTok as @yourspiritualbigsis, had only ever used her powers for good, she...
content:
Inside a podcast studio at Turning Point USA’s headquarters last month, a former witch sat in a pink velvet armchair, telling Alex Clark about the demon that stalked her house. Even though this self-described witch, known on TikTok as @yourspiritualbigsis, had only ever used her powers for good, she believed that practicing sorcery had made her vulnerable to satanic forces. The demon—10, maybe 15 feet tall, whose face had “divots” for eyes—had tormented her, she said, until she spoke the name “Jesus” out loud and became a Christian. 

Clark, whose Culture Apothecary is one of America’s top wellness podcasts, told her guest that she was going to ask “counter questions,” as she does with everyone she interviews. In this case: If the spells she was doing were technically producing good—helping people make money, get pregnant, pass a test—why is that evil? How can Christians tell whether someone has the spiritual gift of prophecy or they’re harnessing dark power? Clark wasn’t concerned about whether sorcery was real—“It is real,” she said—but when her guest brought up the occult sacrifice of babies procured through a sex-trafficking network supported by the government and Hollywood, Clark had no further questions. 

This was just another day in the studio. Since 2024, when she launched her podcast with a mission to “heal a sick culture” and to do so “physically, emotionally, and spiritually,” Clark has welcomed a wild array of guests, united only by their willingness to contradict conventional wisdom and generally accepted facts. Listening to Culture Apothecary, you might hear a regenerative farmer recommend the subcutaneous fat of a “healthy, happy pig” as a miracle skin-care ingredient, a chiropractor talk about testing muscle strength using “homeopathically charged frequencies,” the self-described Christian nationalist Doug Wilson suggest spanking as a form of biblical discipline for children, or leaders in the “Make America Healthy Again” movement disavow vaccines and industrial agriculture. 

On the podcast, Clark positions herself not as an expert but as a question-asking woman of the people. Depending on who you talk with—and I spoke with Clark’s colleagues, her critics, her close friends, her mom—she’s either a powerful force connecting everyday women to the GOP or an agent of chaos. She has been the Republican commentator posting bikini photos while her peers post pictures in cardigans and the single 33-year-old podcasting about child-rearing. By her own account, she is also the contributor at TPUSA, the late Charlie Kirk’s conservative organization, who causes the nonprofit the most trouble with the Trump administration. 

Maggie Shannon for The Atlantic
Alex Clark and a former witch, known on TikTok as @yourspiritualbigsis, during a taping of her podcast, Culture Apothecary, in September

Clark grew up in an evangelical, conservative home in southern Indiana. After high school, she worked at Sephora and took classes at a community college, and planned to transfer to a four-year school for fashion merchandising and journalism. But then she started an internship at a Louisville, Kentucky, radio station, which led to a full-time job as an anchor and the unofficial Millennial-woman correspondent for a morning show. She had always loved pop culture and politics, and came to TPUSA in 2019 so that she could air her conservative views while discussing Dancing With the Stars. Even before Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Donald Trump teamed up, she pivoted to podcasting about wellness because she thought that talking about organic food, herbal medicine, and suspicions about vaccines could bring more women into the GOP. When the MAHA movement came to Washington, Clark’s own profile rose, and soon she had the attention of some of the most powerful men in the country. 

But recently, MAHA and MAGA have started to drift apart. MAHA is failing to draw hordes of voters to Republicans; the Trump administration has failed MAHA on many of the issues Clark cares about. As the rift widens, Clark is stretching to keep a foot on each side and figuring out, if she does have to choose one, how to take her audience of MAHA moms and conservative young women along with her.

Between tapings, Clark ate takeout from a seed-oil-free restaurant as she reviewed podcast transcripts and a spreadsheet of upcoming episodes, reacting to them with facial expressions worthy of a mime. Her team member took notes while she dictated episode titles (“He Was Gay, Then Everything Changed” and “Acetaminophen Before Age 4: What Parents Should Know”). The whole time, she exuded the energy of someone who had incredible gossip to share. The minute I stepped away to check out a rack of Culture Apothecary sweatshirts (Trust Farms, Not Pharma), Clark shrieked. “We’re all peeing our pants, screaming, crying, throwing up,” she said, her eyes wide and made even more dramatic by false lashes. Taylor Swift had just announced a new single. She looked for clues in Swift’s post and predicted that the music video would debut later that week at the MTV Video Music Awards. (She was right.)

Like many 30-something women, she is devoted to Taylor Swift, and, however unfiltered Clark can sometimes seem, like Swift, she aims to make every detail of her world matter. Her studio’s forest-green wallpaper includes illustrations of her preferred remedies for America’s ailing culture: raw milk, steak, butter, wildflowers, hair bows, the Bible. Her podcast-planning spreadsheet is in that same bespoke shade of green, which she developed with graphic designers. (She calls it “Forks, Washington,” after the town made famous in Twilight.) Even her off-the-cuff X posts can be seen as part of her brand—a girl speaking her mind, even if that includes insinuating that Candace Owens performed oral sex on Vladimir Putin. The ads she writes for the show might seem borderline nonsensical—in one ad for a clean-beauty company, for reasons that I do not understand, she includes a monologue about a taxidermied possum who wears a cheerleading uniform and is named Gerald—but according to Clark, that strategy tends to bring high returns for her sponsors. What listener is going to want to skip those? 

Not the “Cuteservatives,” as Clark calls her fandom. They keep tabs on her personal life, too, and at the TPUSA Women’s Leadership Summit in June, she orchestrated an announcement for them. “There’s one thing I haven’t told you guys,” she said. The stage lights went out, and when they came back on, she was standing beside Vance Voetberg, the bespectacled author of the MAHA fitness Substack Running on Butter. On her finger was a diamond ring. “I’m engaged!” The crowd screamed. Later, on Instagram, she described him as her “‘BUTTER’ half.” She has since released a steady stream of content about their small summer wedding at his family home in rural Washington State: a recipe for the prosciutto butter they served, details about the outfits she picked for Voetberg and her maid of honor, and a two-hour interview with her new husband, in which she revealed that she walked down the aisle to Swift’s “You Are In Love” and gifted all of her guests a Jaspr, perhaps the most aesthetically pleasing air purifier in existence.

Maggie Shannon for The Atlantic
Clark and Caroline Lanier, a social-media admin, check out what was probably, if Clark’s obsessions are any indication, a post about Taylor Swift.

Clark is also, like Swift, a woman of distinct eras. For most of her life, she was focused not on health but pop culture. MTV was banned in her childhood home, but when she saw Britney Spears’s “I’m a Slave 4 U” music video at a sleepover, “I was absolutely mesmerized,” she said. She idolized Spears, Christina Aguilera, and Jessica Simpson. She was also so conservative “that she’d make Rush Limbaugh look like a liberal,” her high-school radio and TV teacher, Timothy Dench, told me. 

She knew even then that she wanted an audience made up of young women. She dreamed about being a fashion writer at Teen Vogue or Seventeen, but got the job on a local radio show. Listeners knew her as a fast-food connoisseur and the “Chicken Nugget Princess”—she ate nuggets at least once a day and would peel off the skin, eat that, then turn to the meat. By 2019, she was co-hosting an Indianapolis morning show, but her superiors were telling her to stop bringing up politics on air and on Twitter. She imagined a show that would combine her passions for the GOP and for pop culture—“TMZ and Fox News if they had a baby,” she told me—and pitched it to Charlie Kirk at TPUSA as a way to show women that Republicans could be cool. POPlitics became TPUSA’s first show.

Clark’s wellness era started around 2020. She was skeptical of the COVID shot and never got it, and, after watching the Hulu series Dopesick, became convinced that Big Pharma’s misdeeds were the greatest true-crime story ever told. Practically overnight, she emptied out her fridge and began her transformation into someone who keeps a tiny vial of unrefined sea salt in her purse, sits in front of red light every day, and makes a morning smoothie with six different types of powder, glyphosate-free oats, aloe-vera juice, Cowboy Colostrum, collagen, creatine, strawberries, cherries, pineapple, peaches, and an entire avocado.

And she noticed that her audience was moving toward wellness with her. Whenever she had a guest on to talk about why, say, women should be suspicious of the pill, viewership spiked, so she met with Kirk about rebranding her show around health. “If we are the ones championing these issues, we will grab all the female voters,” she remembers telling him in July 2024. Two weeks before Culture Apothecary was scheduled to debut, she watched RFK Jr. endorse Trump live at a rally in Glendale, Arizona. The crowd was so electric it reminded her of Swift’s Eras Tour. 

A month later, Clark got a standing ovation at the Capitol. Her speech at a Senate roundtable, on behalf of Millennial mothers outraged by food and pharmaceutical corporations harming their children, cemented her as MAHA’s big sister. Sponsors and listeners flocked to Culture Apothecary, and Clark, who now had the attention of both stay-at-home moms and powerful politicians, became the person most visibly fusing MAHA and MAGA for women. 

Over the past year, that union has gotten shakier. Trump’s accord with MAHA—his promise to let RFK Jr. “run wild” on health and food—has been one defining force in his second administration, and the health secretary has managed to remake federal vaccine policy, change the food pyramid, and extract some voluntary commitments from companies about food dye. But many MAHA supporters feel like they were owed more—especially when it came to regulating food and pesticides. The disillusionment has gotten bad enough that one of MAHA’s top leaders, Calley Means, resigned from the Trump administration less than two weeks before the midterms, reportedly out of frustration that the government wasn’t advancing MAHA’s food policy.

Maggie Shannon for The Atlantic
Clark’s bookshelf at her home

Clark, meanwhile, keeps getting angrier. In January, she and other MAHA activists were abruptly disinvited from an event at the Department of Health and Human Services—which they believe was because MAHA had recently launched a petition to fire the head of the EPA. Someone later sent Clark a picture of the check-in table: On the front page of the “Not Permitted List” was her photograph. (In response to a request for comment, HHS referred me to the White House, which did not comment on the disinvitation; a spokesperson told me, “The MAHA coalition has never been stronger or more empowered.”) After the White House and the Supreme Court both came down in favor of the weed killer glyphosate, the chemical that MAHA hates most, Clark headlined a rally outside the Supreme Court Building, wearing a camo jacket that read: I TURN INTO ERIN BROCKOVICH WHEN I’M ANGRY. 

Clark thinks that Trump is a true MAHA believer (despite his love of McDonald’s) and that he’s getting hemmed in by those around him. Before the April rally, Trump met with her and other MAHA leaders, and he kept talking about making an executive order about vaccines. According to Clark, what he described was so extreme that if she shared the details, they would “make him look bad right before midterms.” She believes that his advisers steered him away from it. (Trump did later issue an executive order reducing the number of diseases included in the childhood-vaccination schedule. The White House spokesperson wrote in an email that “President Trump wants to execute on ideas that are durable, long-lasting, and hold up in court to ensure the permanence” of the MAHA movement.) Clark still loves the president, but “I have zero stomach for conservative commentators that all they do is blow the Trump admin,” she said. “Sorry to be crass.” As a Republican, she’d be sad if the GOP loses this cycle, but as a MAHA leader, “then I’d kind of get to flex an ‘I told you so’” about the party needing her audience’s vote.

Clark’s own career doesn’t necessarily hinge on the White House’s approval or MAHA’s political viability. Her wellness episodes were doing well before the MAHA label existed, and she’s proved that she has an instinct for where the conservative movement is going and how to get American women—even those who don’t think of themselves as political—to follow it. Maybe this election will mark the end of an era for MAHA. But Clark is already entering a new one herself.

After a day of taping, Clark took me back to her apartment in Scottsdale, Arizona, where she now lives with her butter half. It still looked like a Millennial girl’s Barbie Dreamhouse: maximalist floral wallpaper, a brocade velvet shower curtain, black-and-white striped accent chairs. A Jaspr air purifier hummed in the corner, and on the floor, her Pekingese, Mochi, ate raw rabbit and organic pumpkin puree from his dog bowl and drank glass-bottled, micro-plastic-tested Loonen water. 

Voetberg had homemade cookies and raw milk waiting for us. He is a national-champion fiddle player and competitive runner, who grew up homeschooled and one of 10 kids. He’d been a fan of Clark’s podcast for years, and after lobbying mutual friends to set them up, he and Clark had their first date last fall, got engaged over Memorial Day weekend, and got married at the end of August. They’d just returned from their Bora-Bora honeymoon. “We have sex now!” She laughed and leaned over their glasses of raw milk to kiss him. 

Clark’s primary goal in life was always to get married and have a family. When, at 23, she appeared on the Fox dating show Coupled, she was so earnest about looking for a husband that the producers told her she needed to relax, she said. Over the years, being single became an occupational hazard. Groypers, the followers of the alt-right leader Nick Fuentes, would DM her pictures of empty egg cartons and tell her that she was useless because she wasn’t married with kids; feminists criticized her for being an unmarried career woman who told other women to focus on their families. 

Now that she’s married, she told me, she will not be a tradwife who embodies a pioneer-esque domestic crunchiness: A nail artist comes to her house every two weeks, and she “wouldn’t last five seconds living more than 10 minutes away from a Sephora.” Nor does she plan to adhere to strict domestic gender roles. Voetberg told me that he takes the lead on household chores; he made those cookies and stepped in to cook chili for dinner while Clark was busy talking with me. She has said she will put family first, but she also wants a career. Between that and her choice to continue using the last name Clark professionally, some people on the right call her a closet feminist. She is not, she told me, and believes that feminism has been a “net negative.” Voetberg chimed in to say that he could see how people might think that she has benefited from the movement. But Clark kept returning to the idea that, overall, feminism had badly served women by pushing them to prioritize their careers over motherhood.

Maggie Shannon for The Atlantic
Alex Clark and her husband, Vance Voetberg, at home with their dog, Mochi  

Her latest Culture Apothecary series—“Wife School”—certainly has gone well beyond any feminist’s comfort zone. In these interviews, she asked married Christian women about how to be a good biblical wife. Guests had tips on household organization but also on giving one’s husband input while still allowing him to be the family’s final decision maker. In one particularly controversial episode, the Christian writer Tilly Dillehay said that, for the health of a marriage, women should have sex with their husbands even when they do not want to. 

If part of MAHA’s success was that it could speak to people across the political spectrum, the issues Clark is now exploring almost certainly don’t. Over chili, Voetberg said that he thought aspects of first-wave feminism had been good. Like the right to vote, I suggested. 

“Don’t get her started on that,” Voetberg said. 

“I’m not gonna advocate to repeal the Nineteenth!” Clark replied, although some people in the MAGAverse insist that the Nineteenth Amendment was a mistake that should, like Roe, be corrected. I asked whether they’d vote as a family, and they started talking about landownership, which was once attached to suffrage, and how the question of who should vote in America was a “giant, giant topic,” as Voetberg put it. Clark joked—maybe?—that she’d love it if she needed her husband’s permission to open a bank account, as American women once did. (Later, she wrote in an email that she and Voetberg had not consciously adopted household voting as a practice—“We just automatically vote the same.”)

When she has kids—and she wants to be pregnant before January—she said that she may look at her newborn and decide to never do another interview again. But her current plan is to keep working. Her audience loved “Wife School,” she said, and she is sensing another groundswell like the one she saw toward health—this one toward human connection, in community and family. Championing those issues could be another way to grab female voters: Moms of all political persuasions can probably agree that, as a recent Culture Apothecary episode argued, “babies don’t need all that STUFF!”—even if many of them are not quite ready to give their husbands the final say on their family decisions, finances, or sex lives.

Knowing how seriously to take Clark’s more provocative stances can be difficult. If Taylor Swift is one of Clark’s idols, so is 1980s and ’90s Howard Stern: He was clever and funny, and wasn’t afraid to be shocking. (“I’m not saying, as a Christian, that I agree with the type of content he was doing,” she said.) For similar reasons, she admires the early days of the sex-and-dating podcast Call Her Daddy, when the hosts graphically detailed their own exploits. “I don’t ever want people to feel comfortable,” Clark said—and her more MAHA-leaning listeners might not be, if she doubles down on a conservative vision of family and femininity. But, she told me, “I love controversy.” It keeps people listening. “Whether you listen to me because you love me, or listen to me because you hate me,” she said, “you’re still a fan either way.”

title: Foie Gras Is Tearing D.C. Apart
summary: In Washington, D.C., voters are thinking more than they usually would about ducks. The most contentious question on the ballot in the nation’s capital this midterm-election cycle is a referendum on foie gras, the extra-fatty liver delicacy made by overfeeding ducks (and sometimes geese) through a tu...
content:
In Washington, D.C., voters are thinking more than they usually would about ducks. The most contentious question on the ballot in the nation’s capital this midterm-election cycle is a referendum on foie gras, the extra-fatty liver delicacy made by overfeeding ducks (and sometimes geese) through a tube stuck down their esophagus. Selling foie gras has been banned in New York City, Pittsburgh, California, India, and Brazil; Target won’t stock it. On Tuesday, D.C. residents will decide: Should their restaurants still be able to serve it?

In the lead-up to the election, anti-foie-gras advocates have imported Olivia Gray, a four-and-a-half-pound male duck from Maryland, to act as their mascot. A Capitol Hill restaurant has countered with a foie-gras tasting menu. A local publication predicted this week that the year’s hottest Halloween costumes would be foie gras–related. Residents are debating the usual moral quandaries of this issue: Is force-feeding ducks a practice so cruel it should be banned? Do people have the right to eat whatever they find delicious? But the real reason the ballot initiative is tearing D.C. apart is that it’s become a proxy for arguments about democracy.

The referendum, known as Initiative 86, would ban “force-feeding a bird for the purpose of enlarging the bird’s liver beyond normal size” within the district, as well as the sale or importation of any products resulting from such practices. It amassed more valid signatures from D.C. residents than any other ballot initiative in the city’s history—more, even, than Initiative 71, the referendum on recreational cannabis that, when passed in 2014, made it possible to (legally) buy a joint four blocks from the White House. Everyone I spoke with, including foie-gras fans, expects Initiative 86 to pass. Ballot measures tend to do well here, and proponents are essentially asking voters to choose duck happiness over a food they’ve probably never eaten.

The pro-ban side, headed by a group called Pro-Animal DC, has spent more than $470,000 lobbying for Initiative 86 to pass. Most of that money was spent this summer on hiring people to collect all of those signatures, a spokesperson for the organization told me. Supporters have been hanging SAVE THE DUCKS posters at Metro stops around the city. Olivia the duck has been making frequent appearances, including co-hosting a panel at George Washington University’s law school. Meghan Abrego, who bought Olivia on eBay when he was just an egg (and Abrego thought he was female), told me that she’s feeling optimistic heading into Election Day. The real question, she said, is not whether the ban will pass, but “What states will pick it up next?”

The anti-ban contingent is not formally organized. Few people seem eager to be targeted as pro–foie gras activists: Bart Hutchins, a local chef who has become the face of the opposition to Initiative 86, told me he has received death threats and has been followed to his car since writing an op-ed opposing the ban in The Washington Post. Hutchins co-owns Butterworth’s, the Capitol Hill restaurant serving the foie-gras tasting menu in protest of the referendum. He told me that the two farms that produce virtually all U.S. foie gras are run ethically; when he has visited the farm he procures Butterworth’s livers from, he said, the ducks don’t actually seem to mind gavage much. Sales from the tasting menu will benefit Hutchins’s Foie Gras Legal Defense Fund, which he says will be put toward mounting a challenge should the ban pass and financially supporting chefs who are fined for continuing to serve the dish, as he intends to do.

This fight is a microcosm of questions about money in politics and what powerful forces might really be behind a grassroots movement. Hutchins and his allies have argued that animal-rights groups are trying to, effectively, force their political views down District residents’ gullets: The initiative is mostly funded by the national organization Pro-Animal Future, which is based in Oregon; Dr. Bronner’s Magic Soaps, headquartered in California, has also contributed money. (Even Olivia is not a D.C. resident.) On the opposing side, a major foie-gras producer based in New York is already rallying its lawyers to challenge the ban if it passes, Axios reported this week.

National organizations fund the activities of local chapters all the time, but D.C. is a particularly attractive city for outside interest groups to fund ballot initiatives: Because of its national prominence, initiatives that pass here are more likely to inspire similar actions across the country. And because its civic-minded voters are packed into a tiny geographic area, gathering petition signatures is easy. Six citizen initiatives have reached the D.C. ballot since 2014, and nearly 90 percent of the total funding for them came from outside the District. As much as they’re arguing about the merits of foie gras, Washingtonians are arguing about astroturfing.

Another popular argument against Initiative 86 is that no one in D.C. should be wasting any time on such a small issue in the first place. Yet I was ready to do my own civic duty. On Wednesday, I made my way to a church to meet Abrego, who was pushing Olivia the duck around in a stroller. Abrego wanted Olivia to appear at a town hall being convened there, but the church wouldn’t let Olivia in, so we stood outside. Some attendees recognized the duck and tried to pet him; D.C.’s Democratic nominee for mayor gave him a high five.

Then I headed from the church to Butterworth’s. Waiting for me were four courses of foie gras, including a Waldorf salad laid on a bed of “foie gras snow” and a “foie gras Twinkie” served with foie-gras ice cream. I’d had foie gras once before on the urging of someone who said the taste would change my life, but I’ve never understood the hype. I still found Butterworth’s version almost disgustingly rich; the duck breast, however, was a star. As I ate, Hutchins made sure I understood that his foie gras comes from ducks that live in open barns and keep to a vegetarian diet; the liver and breast on my plate may have come from the same animal, he said, which helps make farming more sustainable. A man sitting next to me, who said he was a Trump-administration staffer but didn’t volunteer his name, described himself as a foie-gras enthusiast. Nearby, another table started chanting, “Olé, olé, olé, olé; foie gras, foie gras” to the tune of the soccer anthem.

As an on-again, off-again vegetarian, I gravitate toward meat that is so thoroughly estranged from its animal origins that I could imagine it grew on a tree—like a chicken nugget. All in all, the ducks that made my meals at Butterworth’s probably had a better life than most animals I consume. Still, in the lulls in my conversation with Hutchins, my mind would sometimes flash back to Olivia in the stroller, or to the videos I’d seen earlier that day of ducks with metal tubes down their throat. Even if the birds live in an open barn and eat no meat, their livers swell up to 10 times their normal size. After about two weeks of force-feeding, the ducks get so fat they can’t really move.

Foie gras is a low-hanging source of suffering, and using a ballot initiative to bring the issue to a vote seems like a healthy-enough expression of democracy—certainly more healthy than eating as much foie gras as I did. In the Butterworth’s bathroom after my meal, I found myself staring at the rabbits on the wallpaper, feeling sick. Maybe I wasn’t built to handle that much liver. Or maybe the campaign and the backlash had both succeeded in forcing me to think about the political and moral dimensions of my food. That’s democracy at work.

title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
summary: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffectiveCora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has so...
content:
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

content:
Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF

Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

content:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
summary: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatmentThe “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials....
content:
Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment

The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

content:
Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
